answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
1. Scope 2 inventory accounting reforms must remain central and unchanged in importance. A consequential impact metric is not a substitute for robust inventory accounting, and its existence should not dilute, delay, or weaken the proposed Scope 2 improvements
2. A consequential impact metric based on marginal emissions is likely to be overly complex, assumption sensitive, and difficult to standardize, reducing its usefulness for planning, procurement, and credible claims at scale—especially across jurisdictions with different system realities and data availability.
EDF recommends that any consequential impact framework include (1) standardized default datasets published or endorsed by the standard setter, and (2) a clear input hierarchy prioritizing TSO/regulator datasets where available. This is essential to prevent fragmentation and ensure comparability and auditability across reporting entities.
EDF further recommends mandatory disclosures (boundary, timeframe, data sources, method tier, key assumptions, uncertainty) and standardized claim language clarifying what the metric does and does not represent
EDF recommends that the GHG Protocol clarify the distinction between (i) estimating system‑wide emissions impacts for decision‑support purposes, and (ii) making claims about causing emissions reductions. These two applications involve different expectations for baselines, additionality, and disclosure, and clearer differentiation would improve comparability and guard against misinterpretation.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text:
Marginal methods face structural limits that make them unreliable as standardized corporate metrics:
2.1 Multi-technology marginality (dispatch reality)
Many marginal approaches implicitly assume one “marginal technology/fuel” sets the marginal emission rate (e.g., “gas-on-the-margin”). System analysis in France shows marginality is frequently multi technology, shaped by hydro optimization, interconnections, outages, and operational constraints—especially in interconnected systems.
2.2 Data requirements are prohibitive for standard corporate use
A robust marginal signal would require unit-level bid stacks, full merit-order modeling across zones, physical modeling of interconnections (network constraints), and real-time availability of flexible resources. These datasets are generally not accessible and not feasible to operationalize as a universal corporate standard
2.3 Difference-based / statistical approaches are unstable and hard to validate
• Difference-based methods (Δemissions/Δload) can yield erratic gradients because marginal CO₂ does not necessarily track load; residual demand can be driven by non-thermal flexibility
• Statistical methods can be non-representative if they do not capture outages, network constraints, interconnector effects, negative price events, and evolving flexibility resources. Verification and reroducibility are weak without strong disclosure and validation requirements.
